title: US-Canada Trade War Escalates as Talks Collapse and New Tariffs Bite Both Economies
excerpt: Ontario's Doug Ford backs retaliatory tariffs and floats cutting electricity to US states as Canada braces for sweeping new American duties.
body:
• US-Canada trade negotiations collapsed after Washington introduced last-minute demands Canada deemed unacceptable, including restrictions on Ottawa's ability to forge new trade deals
  • Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on US goods effective September 8, with Prime Minister Mark Carney declaring "nothing is off the table" including energy and electricity exports
  • Ontario Premier Doug Ford called for using "every bit of leverage" against the US, including restricting exports of electricity, potash, and energy
  • American consumers face rising prices on toilet paper, lumber, and other goods dependent on Canadian imports

The trade war between the United States and Canada escalated sharply this week after bilateral negotiations broke down, with both sides imposing new tariffs and Canadian leaders signaling willingness to deploy their most powerful economic weapons — including energy and electricity cutoffs — in what has become the deepest rift between the neighbors in decades.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Saturday that Ottawa would retaliate against new US tariffs covering roughly 5% of Canadian exports to America. The retaliatory measures take effect September 8 and could last years, Carney warned, adding support for affected industries.

Talks Collapse Over Last-Minute Demands

Negotiations that had appeared close to a framework deal fell apart when, according to Canadian officials, the US introduced eleventh-hour conditions that went beyond trade into questions of sovereignty. Carney said Washington "proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits to Canada," including curtailing Ottawa's ability to negotiate trade agreements with other nations.

https://x.com/RebelNewsOnline/status/2092276776407822350

A key sticking point was the treatment of larger vehicles. Canada wanted favorable tariff terms proposed for light-duty vehicles to extend to medium- and heavy-duty trucks. The US refused, which Carney said would have excluded Canadian-made models including Ford's F-350, F-450, and F-550 trucks and GM's Silverado, making Canadian production less competitive.

President Trump appeared to confirm the last-minute pivot. Asked about Canadian assertions of late-stage demands, Trump told CNN: "That sounds like me. They have to pay a fair amount. And if they don't pay a fair amount, we won't make a deal."

Ford Pushes for Maximum Pressure

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is Canada's economic engine and home to a major portion of cross-border auto manufacturing, threw his full support behind Carney's firm stance.

"President Trump wants to inflict pain on Canadians. Well unfortunately, we have to inflict pain on Americans."

— Doug Ford, Ontario Premier

Ford said Canada "should be using every bit of leverage we can," including restricting exports of electricity, energy, and potash to the US. Ontario supplies electricity to several American states, including New York, Michigan, and Minnesota — a potentially powerful lever. In March 2025, Ford attempted a 25% electricity export surcharge but withdrew it after Trump threatened to double duties on Canadian steel and aluminum.

British Columbia Premier David Eby echoed the sentiment: "Our politeness should never be mistaken for weakness. We'll always defend ourselves."

American Consumers Feel the Squeeze

The escalation is already translating into real costs for American households. The Guardian reported surging toilet paper prices in the US, driven by tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber that supplies roughly 30% of US demand. Capital Economics analyst Bradley Saunders noted Canada has targeted goods with "readily available domestic alternatives" to maximize pain on American businesses while minimizing harm to Canadian consumers.

Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian cars and auto parts to 50% starting January 1, and in a signal of the deepening personal hostility, proposed renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America."

Broad Canadian Support for Firmness

A Léger Institute poll from August 18 showed 56% of Canadians wanted the government to take a tough stance without making concessions. Even opposition Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre backed retaliation, saying "Canadians must stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks."

Only Alberta, home to major oil and gas reserves, expressed frustration over the failure to reach a deal, with Premier Danielle Smith warning that "tariffs and counter-tariffs hurt businesses, workers, and families on both sides of the border."

For the large Indian-Canadian diaspora — one of Canada's fastest-growing communities with deep ties in both Ontario and British Columbia — the trade war creates uncertainty for businesses operating across the border and for professionals whose livelihoods depend on smooth cross-border economic flows.
